analysis.one_liner: Requires background checks and DOJ verification before selling large ammunition magazines or assault weapons.
analysis.headline: The bill got no committee action and no vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require federally licensed gun dealers to run a criminal background check before selling a large-capacity ammunition magazine — something current law does not require. It would also block sales of assault weapons and large magazines until the Justice Department verified that the buyer truthfully answered questions about any contact with federal law enforcement in the past two years. It was introduced two days after the Orlando nightclub shooting and never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the people best protected would be those in venues where mass shootings occur — schools, nightclubs, workplaces, and public gatherings — because buyers of assault weapons and large magazines would face an added federal screening step designed to catch people with recent federal law-enforcement contact who lie about it. Gun buyers overall would keep their existing rights; only these specific purchases would gain the new check.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a criminal background check before a licensed dealer can sell a large-capacity ammunition feeding device, closing a gap in current law (Section 3 of the bill text [S3]).

Blocks sales of semiautomatic assault weapons and large magazines until the Attorney General verifies the buyer truthfully answered questions about recent federal law-enforcement contact, adding a screening step aimed at would-be attackers (Section 4 [S3]).

analysis.who_pays: Licensed firearms dealers, importers, and manufacturers would carry the new verification duty and could lose sales if the Justice Department does not clear a buyer. Buyers of assault weapons and large magazines would face a slower, more intrusive purchase process.

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on buyers self-reporting federal law-enforcement contact, and it does not explain how the Justice Department could verify an answer of 'none' except by investigation — a process it gives no funding or timeline for [S3].

The definitions it relies on — 'semiautomatic assault weapon' and 'large capacity ammunition feeding device' — come from the expired 1994 statute, so the bill's coverage is tied to a 1994 list rather than a current one [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefit targets the rare but very costly case of an armed attacker, and the cost falls on a narrow set of purchases rather than all gun ownership. The main design weakness is the verification step: the bill orders the Justice Department to confirm buyers' answers but provides no mechanism or timeline for doing so, so its real-world effect is hard to guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, where it stayed without a hearing or a vote until the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Sheila Jackson Lee introduced the bill on June 14, 2016, and the House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
Two days later it was referred again to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations; no further action appears in the record [S5].
Eighteen Democratic cosponsors joined the sponsor; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, gun dealers and manufacturers avoided the new verification duties, and buyers of assault weapons and large magazines face no added screening. Nobody gained the safety protections the bill offered.

for.name: Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 14, 2016 and delivered introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on July 8, 2016 [S1][S5].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral but took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors and cosponsors on record are Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee took no action [S4][S5].

industries.note: Licensed dealers would face a new background-check duty on large magazines and a DOJ verification gate on assault weapons, cutting into unrestricted sales. The industry had no recorded role in this bill's fate; it stalled in committee [S5].
Large-capacity magazines, which current law lets dealers sell without a background check, would become subject to one, adding cost and delay to those sales [S3].
